draft.title: The settlements of 27 and 23 BC
card: Octavian handed his extraordinary powers back to the Senate and the people. The Senate gave him the name Augustus, a title of great dignity and religious respect. It also gave him a large provincial command, which included Spain, Gaul and Syria, where most of the legions were stationed.

Augustus gave up the consulship, which he had held year after year. In return he received tribunicia potestas, the powers of a tribune, for life. He also received imperium maius, a power greater than that of any provincial governor.
These powers let him propose laws, veto the acts of other officials and give orders to governors in every province. He did not need to hold an office such as consul to use them.
Republican offices, the Senate and elections all continued, so the Republic seemed restored. Real control of the provinces, the army and the state lay with Augustus.
draft.remember: Augustus kept the look of the Republic while his powers gave him control.

a.q: Why did the settlements of 27 and 23 BC let Augustus claim he had restored the Republic?
opts: The Senate, offices and elections carried on as before
He gave up his command of the provinces and the army
He was no longer given any powers by the Senate
He held the consulship every year for the rest of his life
a.why: The old institutions continued, so the Republic seemed to be back, while his powers kept real control with him. He did not give up his provincial command in 27 BC, and in 23 BC he gave up the consulship rather than holding it for life.
a.clue: Think about what stayed the same on the surface.

b.q: In 23 BC Augustus gave up the consulship. Why did this not weaken his control of the state?
opts: He gained tribunician power and imperium maius for life
He kept the name Augustus, which gave him legal authority
He was made consul again by the Senate the next year
He had already taken command of the Senate's own armies
b.why: Tribunician power let him propose laws and veto other officials, and imperium maius let him command governors in all provinces. Neither depended on holding the consulship. The name Augustus gave him prestige, not legal power, so it is the tempting wrong answer.
b.clue: Which powers did he receive in return, and for how long?

a.best: The Senate, offices and elections carried on as before

b.best: He gained tribunician power and imperium maius for life

problems.detail: The right option says he gained 'tribunician power and imperium maius for life', which reads as both powers being lifelong. Tribunicia potestas was granted for life in 23 BC, but his imperium and provincial command were granted for set terms and renewed (for example in 18 and 13 BC). The card gives 'for life' only for tribunician power, and the clue ('and for how long?') reinforces the misreading. Reword it, for example: 'He gained tribunician power for life and imperium maius over all governors'.
